title.title: Advanced Power BI
title.subtitle:
From modeling fundamentals to enterprise-grade delivery: an 11-module
arc for analysts, BI developers, and platform owners who need Power BI
to hold up under real production weight.

instructor.name: Brandon Campbell
instructor.credential: M.S., Computer Information Systems — Business Analytics
instructor.bio:
Brandon brings 22 years of experience as a data analyst and the last 9 years focused specifically on
Power BI, helping organizations move from single-author reports to governed, production-grade BI
platforms. He is Microsoft Fabric certified and teaches this program the way he builds it for clients:
with an eye toward what actually holds up once real data, real users, and real deadlines show up.

why.title:
Most Power BI training stops at chart-building.
This one doesn't.
cards: Reports that survive contact with real data
Large fact tables, messy sources, and slow refreshes expose weak modeling fast. This program builds habits that hold up at scale, not just in a demo.
Governance is part of the design, not an afterthought
Row-level security, workspace strategy, and monitoring are taught alongside DAX and visuals -- because a report nobody trusts doesn't get used.
A path from author to platform owner
Learners move from single-report skills toward the operational and architectural judgment that senior BI roles actually require.

arcs.label: ARC · BUILD
arcs.headline: Model it right before you calculate anything
arcs.description: The foundation arc: turning raw, flat data into a trustworthy semantic model and a clean transformation layer -- the two things every later module depends on.

arcs.label: ARC · PRESENT
arcs.headline: Turn a correct model into a report people actually use
arcs.description: The experience arc: report UX that guides rather than overwhelms, a model fast enough to stay that way under load, and analytics that go beyond a static chart.

arcs.label: ARC · PROTECT & OPERATE
arcs.headline: A report that can't be trusted won't be used
arcs.description: The trust arc: locking data down to the right audience, getting a solution live in the Service, and keeping it healthy once real users depend on it.

arcs.label: ARC · SCALE
arcs.headline: From one great report to a platform that scales
arcs.description: The platform arc: capacity and architecture decisions, engineering discipline around Power BI artifacts, and the capstone that proves it all fits together.

modules.title: Advanced Semantic Modeling
modules.description: Turning a flat file into a model that scales, and a schema that survives new requirements.
cards: Star schema from first principles
Fact and dimension design, grain decisions, and why a wide flat table eventually breaks every report built on it.
Relationships that don't fight you
Role-playing dimensions, bridge tables, and composite/DirectQuery model choices with their tradeoffs.
Models built for growth
Handling large fact tables, incremental refresh readiness, and keeping a model maintainable as it scales.

topics.title: Star Schema From First Principles
topics.why: A correct grain and a clean fact/dimension split is the single decision that determines whether every later measure is easy or painful to write.
bullets: Grain First — Decide what one row of the fact table represents before building anything else.
Facts Vs Dimensions — Facts hold numbers and foreign keys; dimensions hold the descriptive context used to slice them.
Flat Tables Break At Scale — A wide flat table works for a demo, but duplicates dimension data and breaks distinct-count and filter logic at scale.
Refactor Live, Not Theory — Refactoring a flat table into a star schema is demonstrated live, not just described.

topics.title: Relationships That Don't Fight You
topics.why: Most 'DAX bugs' reported by learners later in the program are actually relationship design problems -- ambiguous filter paths, wrong cardinality, or a missing role-playing dimension.
bullets: Dedicated Date Tables Per Role — Role-playing dimensions (e.g., order date vs. ship date) need their own dedicated date tables and active relationships.
Bridge Tables Resolve Many-To-Many — Resolve many-to-many relationships without duplicating fact rows.
Import Plus DirectQuery Deliberately — Composite models mix Import and DirectQuery deliberately -- know which tables need which mode and why.
Bidirectional Filtering Is Situational — A tool for specific problems, not a default setting.

topics.title: Models Built For Growth
topics.why: A model that works great with 50,000 test rows can fall over with 50 million production rows -- and by then it's expensive to fix.
bullets: Plan Incremental Refresh Early — Large fact tables need a plan for incremental refresh before they need it operationally.
Cardinality Choices Compound — Cardinality and column choices made early determine how much the model can grow before performance suffers.
Composite And Aggregations — Composite and aggregation strategies let a model stay fast without giving up detail entirely.
Maintainable Means Handoff-Ready — 'Maintainable' means the next person on the team can understand the model too, not just the original author.

topics.title: Role-Playing Dimensions
topics.why: The same fact table often needs to be sliced by more than one date -- order date, ship date, invoice date -- and without a deliberate pattern for that, a model quietly loses the ability to analyze more than one of them at once.
bullets: One Date, Many Business Events — Order date, ship date, and invoice date all relate to “a date,” but they represent different business events and need independent filtering.
Duplicate The Date Dimension — Duplicating the date dimension (one table per role) keeps every relationship simple, active, and easy to reason about.
USERELATIONSHIP As Alternative — The alternative -- one shared date table with USERELATIONSHIP activated per measure -- trades table count for DAX complexity.
Skipping Doesn't Skip The Problem — Skipping this pattern doesn't remove the need for it; it just means the gap shows up later as a broken or missing analysis.

topics.title: Bridge Tables & Composite Models
topics.why: Many-to-many relationships and mixed storage modes are two of the most common reasons a “simple” model turns into a support ticket -- both have a right pattern, and both punish shortcuts.
bullets: Bridge Tables Prevent Duplication — A bridge table resolves many-to-many relationships (a customer in multiple segments) without duplicating fact rows or filtering ambiguity.
Never Wire Bridge To Fact — Never relate a bridge table directly into a fact table -- it filters through its related dimensions, not around them.
Composite Mode Matching — Composite models mix Import and DirectQuery deliberately, matching each table's mode to its actual freshness and performance need.
Judgment Call, Not Default — Both patterns are judgment calls, not defaults -- know when they solve a real problem versus when they add unnecessary complexity.

modules.title: Advanced DAX
modules.description: Getting past copy-pasted measures into real command of filter and row context.
cards: Context, demystified
Filter context vs. row context, and why the same measure can return different numbers on two visuals.
Patterns that hold up under scrutiny
Time intelligence, semi-additive measures, ranking, and calculation groups -- built and explained, not memorized.
Measures that perform
Diagnosing slow DAX, using variables deliberately, and validating logic before layering complexity on top.

topics.title: Context, Demystified
topics.why: Almost every 'my measure gives a wrong number' problem is actually a filter-context or row-context misunderstanding -- once this clicks, most DAX bugs become diagnosable in seconds.
bullets: Row Vs Filter Context — Row context exists inside iterators (SUMX, FILTER); filter context comes from visuals, slicers, and CALCULATE.
CALCULATE Transitions Context — CALCULATE is the tool that transitions row context into filter context -- this is the concept, not the syntax, to teach.
Card Vs Matrix Totals — The same measure can return different totals in a card vs. a matrix because the filter context is different, not because the measure is broken.
Test Measures In Simple Tables — Every new measure should be tested in a simple table visual before trusting it in a complex one.

topics.title: Patterns That Hold Up Under Scrutiny
topics.why: Time intelligence and ranking measures are the ones stakeholders actually stare at during a business review -- they need to be right and explainable, not just plausible-looking.
bullets: Marked Date Table Foundation — Time intelligence functions rely on a proper, contiguous marked date table -- this is where Module 1's foundation pays off.
Semi-Additive Needs Explicit Handling — Semi-additive measures (e.g., ending balance) need explicit handling; they don't sum correctly across time by default.
RANKX With Hand-Checked Validation — Dynamic Top N/ranking measures should be built with RANKX and validated against a static, hand-checked example.
Calculation Groups Reduce Duplication — Calculation groups reduce measure duplication when the same time-intelligence logic applies to many base measures.

topics.title: Measures That Perform
topics.why: A correct measure that takes eight seconds to render is still a support ticket waiting to happen -- performance is part of correctness in a production report.
bullets: Name Steps With VAR — Use VAR to name intermediate results -- it clarifies logic and can prevent redundant evaluation.
Diagnose Before Guessing — Diagnose slow measures with the query plan and Performance Analyzer before guessing at a fix.
Iterators Are Common Culprits — Iterators (SUMX, FILTER) over large tables are the most common source of slow DAX -- know when a simpler aggregation will do.
Correct First, Then Fast — Validate correctness first, then optimize -- a fast wrong answer is worse than a slow right one.

topics.title: Filter Modification Functions
topics.why: ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLEXCEPT, and TREATAS are the tools that let a measure deliberately override the filter context around it -- used well, they solve real business questions; used carelessly, they're where “% of total” measures quietly go wrong.
bullets: ALL And REMOVEFILTERS Clear Everything — ALL and REMOVEFILTERS clear filters entirely, which is exactly what a “% of grand total” measure needs and exactly what breaks a measure that should stay filtered.
ALLEXCEPT Keeps Specific Filters — ALLEXCEPT keeps specific filters while clearing everything else -- useful, but easy to misuse if the “kept” columns aren't chosen deliberately.
KEEPFILTERS Adds, Not Replaces — KEEPFILTERS adds filters instead of replacing them, a subtle distinction that changes results inside CALCULATE.

TREATAS For Virtual Relationships — TREATAS applies a filter from one table's values onto another without a physical relationship -- powerful, but it should be a deliberate exception, not a workaround for bad model design.

topics.title: Production-Ready DAX
topics.why: A measure that's correct in isolation can still be a production risk if nobody validated it against edge cases or documented what “correct” even means for that number.
bullets: Catch Cheap Mistakes Early — Common mistakes -- implicit measures, unhandled blanks, and divide-by-zero -- are cheap to catch before a report ships and expensive to explain after it doesn't.
Validate Against Hand-Checked Examples — Check every new measure against a hand-checked example, not just a plausible-looking total.
Document Non-Obvious Logic — Document the business logic and assumptions behind non-obvious measures so the next author doesn't have to reverse-engineer them.
Trustworthy And Maintainable — “Production-ready” means a measure a stakeholder can trust and a teammate can maintain -- not just one that returns a number.

modules.title: Advanced Power Query
modules.description: Building a transformation layer that's traceable, testable, and reusable -- not a black box.
cards: Staged, parameterized pipelines
Parameters for source switching, staged queries, and functions that eliminate copy-pasted steps.
Query folding and performance
Understanding when a query pushes work back to the source, and when it silently stops.
Data quality as a first-class step
Error-review patterns and cleansing functions that make bad rows visible instead of silently dropped.

topics.title: Staged, Parameterized Pipelines
topics.why: A query pipeline built from named, staged steps and parameters can move from dev to test to production data sources in minutes instead of a manual rebuild.
bullets: Parameters Isolate Environments — Parameters isolate source paths/connections so the same pipeline works across environments.
Staged Query Layers — Staging queries (raw → staged → final) make each transformation step reviewable in isolation.
Custom Functions Eliminate Duplication — Custom functions eliminate copy-pasted steps across similar queries -- one function, many callers.
Step Names As Documentation — Descriptive step names turn the Applied Steps pane into documentation, not a mystery.

topics.title: Query Folding And Performance
topics.why: When folding breaks silently, the query still returns correct results -- it just pulls every row into memory and transforms it locally, which can turn a 30-second refresh into a 30-minute one.
bullets: Folding Pushes Work Down — Folding means Power Query translates steps into a query the source executes natively (e.g., SQL).
Steps That Break Folding — Certain steps (custom columns with complex logic, some merges) can break folding -- know which ones.
View Native Query Often — Use 'View Native Query' or step-by-step inspection to confirm folding is still happening after each transformation.
Deliberate Local Processing — When folding isn't possible, decide deliberately where local processing happens rather than discovering it by accident.

topics.title: Data Quality As A First-Class Step
topics.why: Silently dropped or coerced bad rows are one of the most dangerous failure modes in a BI solution -- the report looks fine and the numbers are simply wrong.
bullets: Explicit Error-Review Query — Build an explicit error-review query that captures rows failing type conversion or business rules instead of discarding them.
Reusable Cleansing Functions — Cleansing functions (e.g., text normalization) should be reusable and applied consistently across sources.
Decide The Invalid-Row Policy — Decide and document what happens to invalid rows: excluded, corrected, or flagged for manual review.
Errors Are A Report Artifact — Treat the error-review query as a report artifact stakeholders can see, not just a developer scratch pad.

topics.title: Native Queries and Source Systems
topics.why: Understanding what a source system actually receives -- not just what Power Query displays -- is what separates a query that scales from one that quietly overloads its source every refresh.
bullets: See The Actual Statement — “View Native Query” shows the exact statement sent to the source, confirming folding is happening and revealing what the source will actually execute.
Not Every Source Folds — Some source systems (APIs, flat files) can't fold at all -- know which of your sources can and design around the ones that can't.
Security Checkpoint Too — Native query review is also a security checkpoint: it shows exactly what credentials and permissions a refresh depends on.
Respect Source System Limits — Treat the source system's own limits (rate limits, connection pools) as a real design constraint, not an afterthought.

topics.title: Incremental Refresh Preparation
topics.why: Incremental refresh only works if the query is built to support it from the start -- retrofitting it onto an existing pipeline after the fact usually means redesigning the query, not just flipping a setting.
bullets: Reliable Last-Modified Column — A reliable, indexed “last modified” or date column is the foundation every incremental refresh policy depends on.
Wire RangeStart And RangeEnd — Parameters that define the refresh window (RangeStart/RangeEnd) need to be wired into the query's filtering logic, not just declared.
Confirm Folding After Parameters — Confirm the query still folds correctly once range parameters are added -- a parameter that breaks folding defeats the purpose.
Foundation For Module 5 — Preparing for incremental refresh here is what makes Module 5's refresh strategy possible later.

modules.title: Report Design & UX
modules.description: Designing navigation and interaction, not just placing visuals on a canvas.
cards: Guided interaction patterns
Drillthrough, bookmarks, custom tooltips, and navigation that leads users somewhere intentional.
Hierarchies, drill & groups
Drill-down, drill-across, and custom groups/bins that let one visual answer questions at multiple levels of detail.
Flexible by design
Field parameters and dynamic titles that let one report answer several questions instead of one.
Built for every screen and every user
Mobile-optimized layouts, conditional formatting, and an accessibility pass before anything ships.

topics.title: Guided Interaction Patterns
topics.why: Users don't read instructions -- the report itself has to teach them where to click and what will happen when they do.
bullets: Drillthrough For Detail — Drillthrough pages answer 'tell me more about this one thing' without cluttering the main view.
Bookmarks Capture State — Bookmarks capture a specific state (filters, visibility, selections) that can be recalled with one click.
Tooltips Add Context — Custom tooltips replace a bare number with context -- a mini visual, a trend, a comparison.
Make Navigation Obvious — Navigation should be visibly obvious, not just technically functional -- users won't discover a hidden feature.

topics.title: Hierarchies, Drill & Groups
topics.why: A hierarchy lets one visual answer 'show me the summary' and 'show me exactly why' without building a separate visual or page for every level of detail.
bullets: Build Hierarchies Once — Hierarchies (e.g., Category > Subcategory > Product) are built once in the model and reused across every visual that needs them.
Drill Up And Down — Drill-down moves a single visual deeper into its own hierarchy; drill-up reverses it -- both stay on the same visual.
Drill Across Visuals — Drill-across sends a selection to a different visual or page (via drillthrough or cross-report drill), showing related detail in a different context.
Groups And Bins — Groups and bins collapse many raw values into meaningful buckets (an 'Other' category, price bands) without changing the underlying data.
Show Next Level Deliberately — Turn on 'Show next level' and 'Expand all' deliberately -- they change how a user explores versus click-drills one level at a time.

topics.title: Flexible By Design
topics.why: Field parameters turn one page into several reports' worth of value, which matters enormously when report sprawl is already a real governance problem in most organizations.
bullets: Field Parameters Swap Fields — Field parameters let users swap the measure or dimension a visual is built on, without duplicating pages.
Dynamic Titles Reflect Selection — Dynamic titles that reflect the current selection make a flexible page still feel intentional, not generic.
Fewer, More Flexible Pages — Fewer, more flexible pages are easier to maintain and govern than many near-duplicate ones.
Sensible Defaults Still Matter — Flexibility should still have sensible defaults -- 'infinitely customizable' isn't the same as 'usable.'

topics.title: Built For Every Screen And Every User
topics.why: A report that only works well on a widescreen monitor for a sighted user with perfect color vision has quietly excluded a meaningful share of its actual audience.
bullets: Mobile Is A Separate Pass — Mobile layout is a separate design pass, not an automatic resize of the desktop layout.
Formatting With Meaning — Conditional formatting should communicate meaning (status, threshold, direction), not just add color.
Accessibility Review Before Ship — An accessibility review checks tab order, alt text, and color contrast before a report ships.
Design For Edge Cases — Design for the edge-case user (screen reader, phone, colorblind) and the default experience improves for everyone.

topics.title: Audience-Driven Design
topics.why: A report built for “everyone” usually serves no one well -- an executive scanning for one number and an analyst investigating a trend need fundamentally different layouts, not the same page with more filters.
bullets: Start With The Audience — Start every report with a specific primary audience and their first question, not a blank canvas and a list of available fields.
Shared Model, Different Layouts — An executive summary page and an analyst detail page can share a model without sharing a layout.
Match The Audience — Visual density, color use, and interactivity should match how sophisticated and how busy the actual audience is.
Ask Who And Why First — Ask “who opens this and what do they need to decide” before placing a single visual.

topics.title: Slicers and Filters as Design Tools
topics.why: Slicers and filters are the primary way users interact with a report -- placed and scoped carelessly, they create confusion (does this filter the whole page or just one visual?) faster than any visual design choice.
bullets: Filter Scope Is A Choice — Filter scope (visual, page, or report level) should be a deliberate choice, communicated clearly, not left to default behavior.
Sync Slicers Carefully — Sync slicers across pages only when the same filter should logically apply everywhere -- otherwise it creates surprising side effects.
Too Many Slicers — Too many slicers on one page is itself a design smell -- it often means the report is trying to answer too many questions at once.
Default Filter State Matters — A well-designed default filter state matters as much as the slicers themselves -- users judge a report by what they see first.

modules.title: Performance Optimization
modules.description: Finding out why a report is slow before guessing how to fix it.
cards: Evidence before optimization
Performance Analyzer baselines and DAX Studio comparisons -- measure first, then change one thing.
Model size is a design decision
Cardinality reduction, aggregation tables, and composite model choices that shrink refresh and query time.
Refresh strategy at scale
Incremental refresh policy design and the licensing/capacity tradeoffs that come with it.

topics.title: Evidence Before Optimization
topics.why: Optimizing based on a guess wastes time and can make performance worse -- a baseline turns 'this feels slow' into 'this specific visual takes 4.2 seconds because of this specific query.'
bullets: Break Down Load Time — Performance Analyzer breaks down visual load time into DAX query time, visual display time, and other time.
DAX Studio For Isolation — DAX Studio shows the underlying query and server timings for a measure in isolation.
Change One Thing At A Time — Capture the baseline, change exactly one thing, and re-measure -- don't change five things and hope.
Not Every Problem Is DAX — Some 'performance problems' are actually visual count or interaction problems, not DAX problems at all.

topics.title: Model Size Is A Design Decision
topics.why: Reducing an unnecessary column's cardinality or removing an unused column can shrink a model more than any DAX tweak -- and it costs nothing at query time once it's done.
bullets: Watch High-Cardinality Columns — High-cardinality columns (e.g., unique IDs, full timestamps) are expensive -- keep only what's needed at the grain required.
Aggregation Tables For Speed — Aggregation tables serve common high-level queries fast while detail tables remain available for drill-down.
Composite For Freshness — Composite models let a subset of tables use DirectQuery for freshness while the rest stay in-memory for speed.
Column Removal Wins — Column removal and cardinality reduction are usually the highest-leverage, lowest-risk performance wins available.

topics.title: Refresh Strategy At Scale
topics.why: A report that takes 20 minutes to refresh isn't just annoying -- it delays every downstream decision that depends on the data being current, and it can hit capacity or gateway limits outright.
bullets: Incremental Refresh Partitions — Incremental refresh only reprocesses new or changed partitions instead of the entire table.
Match Source Change Patterns — Refresh policy design (partition ranges, detection columns) has to match how the source data actually changes.
Licensing Sets The Ceiling — Licensing and capacity tier determine what refresh options and frequency are even available.
Document The Strategy — A refresh strategy should be documented, not just configured -- the next owner needs to understand why it's set up this way.

topics.title: Visual and Rendering Performance
topics.why: Some “slow report” complaints have nothing to do with DAX or the model at all -- too many visuals on a page, unnecessary interactions, and heavy custom visuals can dominate load time on their own.
bullets: Every Visual Fires A Query — Every visual on a page issues its own query -- fewer, more purposeful visuals often outperform a dense dashboard of small ones.
Custom Visuals Cost Time — Custom and R/Python visuals typically render slower than native visuals -- use them where they add real value, not by default.
Trim Cross-Highlighting — Disabling unnecessary cross-highlighting and interactions reduces the number of queries fired on every click.
Confirm The Real Bottleneck — Performance Analyzer separates DAX time from visual display time -- confirm which one is actually the bottleneck before optimizing the wrong thing.

topics.title: DirectQuery and Hybrid Patterns
topics.why: DirectQuery trades import-mode speed for live data -- a hybrid (composite) model lets a team choose that tradeoff table-by-table instead of accepting it for an entire model.
bullets: DirectQuery Runs Live — DirectQuery queries the source live on every interaction, so source performance becomes the report's performance.
Composite For Hybrid Freshness — Composite models let high-value, fast-changing tables use DirectQuery while stable, high-volume tables stay in Import mode.
Aggregations Front Detail — Aggregation tables can sit in Import mode in front of a DirectQuery detail table, serving common queries fast while keeping full detail available.
Choose For Real Freshness Needs — Choose DirectQuery for freshness requirements that actually exist today, not as a default “just in case” setting.

modules.title: Advanced Analytics & AI
modules.description: Going past the default chart into scenario modeling and AI-assisted analysis -- with eyes open about where it's available.
cards: What-if, not just what-happened
Parameter-driven scenario analysis that lets stakeholders test assumptions live in the report.
The analytics visual toolkit
Decomposition trees, forecasting, and key influencers for driver analysis beyond a trend line.
AI-assisted authoring, used deliberately
Python/R visuals and Azure ML integration explored with a clear-eyed view of cloud and tenant availability.

topics.title: What-If, Not Just What-Happened
topics.why: A what-if parameter turns a static report into a decision tool -- stakeholders can test 'what if margin improves 2%' live instead of asking an analyst to rebuild the report for every scenario.
bullets: Parameter-Driven Scenarios — What-if parameters generate a slicer-driven value that flows into a measure's calculation.
Show The Before And After — Pair the parameter with a clear before/after visual so the impact of the scenario is immediately obvious.
Document The Assumption — Document the assumption behind the scenario -- a number without its underlying assumption is easy to misread.
Universally Available Analytics — This is the most universally available advanced analytics feature -- it works the same way across clouds.

topics.title: The Analytics Visual Toolkit
topics.why: Decomposition trees, forecasting, and key influencers answer 'why' and 'what's next,' not just 'what happened' -- that's a fundamentally different, higher-value conversation with stakeholders.
bullets: Decomposition Trees Explore Drivers — Decomposition trees let users explore what's driving a metric interactively, without pre-building every breakdown.
Forecasting With Intervals — Forecasting visuals project a trend forward with a confidence interval, not a false-precision single number.
Key Influencers — Key influencers surface which factors most affect an outcome, using statistical analysis under the hood.
Confirm Cloud Availability — These visuals are commonly Commercial-cloud features -- confirm availability before building a delivery plan around them.

topics.title: AI-Assisted Authoring, Used Deliberately
topics.why: Python/R visuals and Azure ML integration open real analytical power, but they also introduce dependencies (package policy, network, identity, region) that can quietly break a report outside a Commercial tenant.
bullets: Python And R Visuals — Python/R visuals require Desktop configuration and depend on organizational package policy in the Service.
Azure ML Prerequisites — Azure Machine Learning integration depends on cloud, region, workspace, network, and identity configuration all lining up.
Validated, Not Assumed — Treat these features as 'available if validated,' not 'available by default' -- confirm in the actual delivery tenant.
Teach The Concept Anyway — Where these aren't available, teach the underlying concept and workflow even if the hands-on lab isn't possible.

topics.title: Anomaly Detection
topics.why: A trend line shows what happened; anomaly detection flags the one point that doesn't fit the pattern -- often the exact moment a stakeholder actually needed to know about.
bullets: Statistical, Not Just Visual — Anomaly detection highlights points in a time series that fall outside an expected statistical range, not just visually obvious spikes.
Clean Time Series Required — It works best on a clean, contiguous time series -- the same date table discipline from Module 1 pays off here too.
Humans Explain Anomalies — Flagged anomalies need a human explanation attached (a promotion, an outage, a data error) -- the feature finds them, it doesn't explain them.
Prompt Investigation, Don't Decide — Use it to prompt investigation, not to make an automated judgment call the business should make itself.

topics.title: Copilot in Power BI and Fabric
topics.why: Copilot can draft a report, summarize a page, or explain a visual in plain language -- but it works from the model it's given, so a well-governed semantic model is what makes its answers trustworthy instead of just plausible-sounding.
bullets: Model Quality Drives Copilot — Copilot's output quality depends directly on model quality -- clear naming, descriptions, and a clean star schema from Module 1 make it dramatically more useful.
First Draft, Not Final — Treat Copilot-generated visuals and summaries as a fast first draft to review, not a final, unreviewed answer.
Confirm Tenant Availability — Availability and tenant settings for Copilot features vary by licensing and cloud -- confirm what's enabled before planning a delivery around it.
Governance Still Applies — Copilot changes how reports get built, not what makes a report correct -- validation and governance still apply.

modules.title: Security Design
modules.description: Designing row-level security like an architecture decision, not a checkbox.
cards: Static and dynamic RLS
Building roles that scale from a handful of regions to a dynamic, user-driven security model.
Testing security like a user would
Validating roles in Desktop and Service, not just trusting the DAX filter is correct.
Where Build permission fits in
Understanding what elevated permissions expose, and designing around that risk deliberately.

topics.title: Static And Dynamic RLS
topics.why: Choosing the wrong RLS pattern for the organization's scale means either constant manual role maintenance or an overengineered dynamic model nobody can audit.
bullets: Static RLS Is Simple — Static RLS assigns fixed filter values per role -- simple, auditable, but doesn't scale past a small number of roles.
Dynamic RLS Uses Identity — Dynamic RLS derives the filter from the logged-in user's identity against a security mapping table.
Dynamic Scales, With Tradeoffs — Dynamic RLS scales far better but is harder to test and requires a well-maintained user-to-permission mapping table.
Choose For Actual Group Count — Choose the pattern based on how many distinct access groups actually exist today and realistically will in two years.

topics.title: Testing Security Like A User Would
topics.why: An RLS role that looks correct in the DAX editor can still leak data in practice -- the only real test is viewing the report exactly as that user would see it.
bullets: View As Roles In Desktop — Use 'View As Roles' in Desktop to preview the report exactly as a given role would experience it.
Test In The Service Too — Test in the Service too -- Desktop and Service can behave differently depending on gateway and dataset configuration.
Cover Every Page And Tooltip — Check every visual and every drillthrough/tooltip page under each role, not just the main landing page.
Negative Testing Matters — Negative testing matters: confirm a role can't see what it shouldn't, not just that it can see what it should.

topics.title: Where Build Permission Fits In
topics.why: Build permission on a dataset is powerful and easy to grant too broadly -- and because it bypasses report-level RLS enforcement in certain connection scenarios, understanding it is core to real security design, not a footnote.
bullets: What Build Permission Grants — Build permission lets a user create new reports against the shared dataset directly.
Live Connections Can Bypass RLS — Depending on connection type, a user with Build permission and a live connection can potentially see data outside their intended RLS scope.
Grant Sparingly, Understand Fully — Grant Build deliberately and sparingly, understanding exactly what it unlocks for that user.
Audit Build Grants Ongoing — Document who has Build permission on sensitive datasets as part of the ongoing governance review, not a one-time setup step.

topics.title: Object-Level Security (OLS)
topics.why: RLS hides rows; OLS hides entire tables or columns -- without it, a sensitive column (salary, SSN, margin) is visible to anyone with access to the table, no matter how well the rows are filtered.
bullets: OLS Restricts Tables And Columns — OLS restricts visibility of specific tables or columns per role, independent of any row-level filtering.
Measures Can Leak Hidden Columns — A hidden column can still leak through a measure that references it -- audit dependent measures before hiding a column.
Configured Per Role — OLS is configured per role in the model, the same place static and dynamic RLS roles live.
Combine RLS And OLS — Combine RLS and OLS deliberately when a role needs both row-level and column-level restriction -- they solve different problems together.

topics.title: Sensitivity Labels and Purview
topics.why: A perfectly secured report can still leak data the moment someone exports it to Excel or emails a screenshot -- sensitivity labels and Purview extend protection past the report itself.
bullets: Labels Travel With The Data — Sensitivity labels (Public, Confidential, Highly Confidential) travel with the data even after export, not just inside the report.
Enforce Export Restrictions — Labels can restrict or watermark export, and enforce encryption on downloaded files.
Purview Sees The Tenant — Microsoft Purview gives visibility into where sensitive data actually lives and flows across the tenant, not just inside one workspace.
Consistency Or Nothing — Labeling is only effective if it's applied consistently -- an unlabeled sensitive dataset is invisible to every downstream control.

modules.title: Service Deployment
modules.description: Getting from a working PBIX/PBIP to a solution real people depend on daily.
cards: Publishing with intent
Workspace strategy, App packaging, and deployment pipelines instead of ad hoc publish clicks.
Refresh you can trust
Scheduled refresh, gateway considerations, and troubleshooting failures before users notice them.
A repeatable release process
Moving a report from dev to test to production with a process, not tribal memory.

topics.title: Publishing With Intent
topics.why: A workspace strategy decided in advance prevents the all-too-common outcome of dozens of ungoverned personal workspaces holding business-critical reports nobody officially owns.
bullets: Plan Workspace Structure First — Workspace structure (by team, by domain, by environment) should be decided before reports start accumulating in it.
Apps Package Curated Content — Apps package a curated, permissioned view of workspace content for end users, separate from author-facing workspace access.
Deployment Pipelines Across Stages — Deployment pipelines move content through dev/test/production stages without manual re-publishing at each step.
Publish With An Owner — Publishing should be a deliberate act with an owner, not an ad hoc click whenever a report 'feels done.'

topics.title: Refresh You Can Trust
topics.why: A dashboard nobody trusts because it silently failed to refresh last Tuesday is worse than no dashboard at all -- it actively misleads decisions.
bullets: Monitor, Don't Just Schedule — Scheduled refresh needs monitoring, not just configuration -- know how failures are surfaced and to whom.
Gateways Fail Silently — Gateway configuration and credentials are common points of silent failure; document them clearly.
Check Refresh Proactively — Build a habit of checking refresh history proactively rather than waiting for a user to report stale data.
Alerts To Someone Who Acts — Failure alerts should go to someone who can act, not just to an inbox nobody monitors.

topics.title: A Repeatable Release Process
topics.why: Moving a report from 'my test version' to 'the production version everyone relies on' without a defined process is how untested changes end up in front of executives.
bullets: Separate Dev, Test, Production — Define distinct dev, test, and production environments -- even a lightweight version of this separation helps.
Release Checklist Beats Memory — A release checklist (RLS tested, refresh validated, visuals reviewed) turns tribal memory into a repeatable process.
Same Outcome Every Time — Deployment pipelines or a documented manual process should produce the same outcome regardless of who runs it.
Process Prevents Skipping — The goal isn't heavyweight process for its own sake -- it's making sure nothing important gets skipped under deadline pressure.

topics.title: Shared Semantic Models and Thin Reports
topics.why: Rebuilding the same measures in every new report is how organizations end up with five different definitions of “revenue” -- a shared model with thin reports on top of it is the fix.
bullets: One Model, Many Reports — A shared semantic model is built and governed once; multiple thin reports connect live to it instead of duplicating its logic.
Thin Reports Prevent Drift — Thin reports contain only visuals and layout -- no local measures, no local tables, no drift from the source model.
One Number, Everywhere — This pattern is what makes “one number, everywhere” achievable at an organizational scale, not just within a single report.
Model Change Management — Changes to the shared model instantly and consistently affect every connected report -- powerful, but it raises the bar on model change management.

topics.title: Endorsement: Promoted vs Certified
topics.why: Without endorsement, every dataset and report looks equally trustworthy in the Service -- endorsement is the visible signal that tells users which ones actually are.
bullets: Promoted Is Self-Service — “Promoted” means the content owner vouches for it -- a lightweight, self-service signal of quality.
Certified Passes Formal Review — “Certified” means it passed a formal organizational review -- a stronger signal reserved for content that meets a defined bar.
Gate Certification Seriously — Certification should be gated by an actual review process, not handed out to keep authors happy.
Endorsement Aids Discovery — Endorsement status directly affects discoverability -- users can search and filter for certified content first.

modules.title: Monitoring, Administration & Governance
modules.description: Running Power BI like a platform, not a pile of individually-managed reports.
cards: Usage as a signal
Usage metrics and refresh history read as operational data, not vanity numbers.
Tenant settings with intention
Understanding what each governance lever controls and who should be allowed to change it.
An operations runbook that outlives you
Documenting the processes so governance survives a team change, not just a tenure.

topics.title: Usage As A Signal
topics.why: Usage metrics tell you which reports are actually load-bearing for the organization and which ones are quietly abandoned -- both are equally important to know.
bullets: Usage Metrics Reports — Usage metrics reports show views, unique users, and trends over time per report and workspace.
Declining Usage Is A Signal — A report with declining usage may be broken, outdated, or simply superseded -- investigate rather than assume.
Fresh And Actually Used — Refresh history read alongside usage tells you whether a heavily used report is also a reliably fresh one.
Retire With Data — Use usage data to justify retiring reports, not just to justify building new ones.

topics.title: Tenant Settings With Intention
topics.why: Tenant settings control organization-wide capabilities like external sharing and export -- getting them wrong is either a security exposure or an unnecessary blocker on legitimate work.
bullets: Owner Per Setting — Every tenant setting should have a known owner and a documented reason for its current configuration.
Export Vs Security Tension — Export and sharing settings are common areas where security and usability pull in opposite directions.
Review Before Changing — Changes to tenant settings should go through the same review rigor as any other security-relevant change.
Scheduled Setting Reviews — Review tenant settings on a schedule -- they drift out of alignment with actual organizational need over time.

topics.title: An Operations Runbook That Outlives You
topics.why: Governance that lives only in one administrator's head disappears the day that person changes roles -- a written runbook is what makes governance durable.
bullets: Document The Why — Document the 'why' behind key decisions (workspace structure, tenant settings, RLS patterns), not just the 'what.'
Specific Enough To Follow Alone — A runbook should be specific enough that a new administrator could follow it without asking the previous owner.
Update On A Cadence — Review and update the runbook on a cadence -- stale documentation is almost as risky as no documentation.
Runbook Is A Governed Artifact — Treat the runbook itself as a governed artifact with an owner and a review date.

topics.title: Activity and Audit Logs
topics.why: When something goes wrong -- a dataset deleted, permissions changed, data exported unexpectedly -- the activity log is the only reliable record of who did what and when.
bullets: Activity Log Coverage — The activity log captures user actions across the tenant: views, exports, sharing changes, and administrative actions.
Know Queries Before Incidents — Audit logs support both security investigations and compliance reporting -- know how to query them before an incident, not during one.
Log Retention Is Governance — Retention and access to these logs is itself a governance decision that needs an owner and a documented policy.
Review, Don't Just React — Regularly reviewing logs (not just reacting to them) surfaces risky patterns -- like broad, unexpected sharing -- before they become incidents.

topics.title: Purview and Data Loss Prevention
topics.why: Governance that only works inside Power BI has a blind spot -- Purview and DLP extend policy enforcement to wherever the data actually travels next, including outside the tenant.
bullets: Purview Beyond Power BI — Microsoft Purview catalogs sensitive data across the broader Microsoft 365 and Azure estate, not just Power BI content.
DLP Acts Automatically — Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies can automatically detect and act on sensitive data leaving approved boundaries.
Labels Plus DLP — Combining sensitivity labels with DLP turns a passive label into an enforced, active control.
Organization-Wide Compliance — This is where Power BI governance connects to organization-wide compliance -- it's not a Power BI-only concern.

modules.title: Premium, Fabric & Capacity Architecture
modules.description: Choosing the right capacity and architecture before scale forces the decision for you.
cards: Capacity models compared
Shared, Premium, and Fabric capacity tradeoffs mapped to real workload patterns, not just price sheets.
Fabric-aware design
OneLake and Direct Lake concepts, and what they change about how a model should be built.
Planning for growth, not just today
Architecture decisions that anticipate the next 10x of data volume and user count.

topics.title: Capacity Models Compared
topics.why: The 'right' capacity tier depends on workload shape (refresh frequency, concurrent users, dataset size), not just budget -- picking based on price alone often causes a costly re-architecture later.
bullets: Shared Capacity Has Limits — Shared capacity is fine for smaller, less demanding workloads but has real limits on refresh frequency and dataset size.
Premium And Fabric Unlock Scale — Premium/Fabric capacity unlocks larger datasets, more frequent refresh, and dedicated performance, at a cost tradeoff.
Map Workload To Tier — Map actual workload characteristics (concurrency, data volume, refresh needs) to capacity tiers before committing.
Migration Isn't Free — Capacity decisions are reversible but not free -- migrating workloads after the fact has real cost and effort.

topics.title: Fabric-Aware Design
topics.why: OneLake and Direct Lake change some long-held assumptions about when data needs to be imported versus queried live -- modeling decisions made without this context can be needlessly conservative.
bullets: OneLake Shared Storage — OneLake provides a single, shared storage layer that multiple Fabric workloads can reference without duplication.
Direct Lake Performance — Direct Lake mode can deliver near-Import-mode performance while querying data directly from OneLake.
Don't Rebuild Everything — Not every existing modeling pattern needs to change for Fabric -- but new projects should evaluate it deliberately.
Fabric Adoption Prerequisites — Fabric adoption is itself an architecture decision with tenant, licensing, and readiness prerequisites to confirm first.

topics.title: Planning For Growth, Not Just Today
topics.why: An architecture that comfortably handles today's data volume and user count can become the org's biggest technical debt the moment either one grows tenfold.
bullets: Plan For 10x Scale — Ask 'what does this look like at 10x scale' as a standard part of any new architecture decision.
Know The Breaking Points — Capacity, refresh strategy, and model design all have breaking points -- know roughly where they are before hitting them.
Review On A Cadence — Plan a capacity/architecture review cadence rather than only revisiting it after something breaks.
Proactive Beats Reactive — Growth planning is cheaper before the system is load-bearing than after -- treat it as proactive work, not reactive firefighting.

topics.title: XMLA Endpoint
topics.why: The XMLA endpoint turns a Power BI semantic model into something external tools can connect to directly -- it's what makes enterprise-grade model management (version control, scripted deployment, external validation) possible at all.
bullets: XMLA Connects External Tools — XMLA read/write access lets tools like Tabular Editor and ALM Toolkit connect to a published model exactly like a tabular database.
Enables DevOps On The Service — This is the mechanism that makes Module 11's external-tool and DevOps workflows possible on models already in the Service.
Read-Only For Other BI Tools — Read-only XMLA access also lets other BI tools query a Power BI model as a data source.
Premium Or Fabric Required — XMLA access requires Premium or Fabric capacity and the right tenant setting -- confirm both before planning around it.

topics.title: Paginated Reports
topics.why: Some deliverables -- regulatory filings, invoices, multi-page statements -- need pixel-perfect, printable layouts that a standard Power BI canvas was never designed to produce.
bullets: Print-Ready Layouts — Paginated reports (built in Report Builder) render precise, print-ready layouts that flow correctly across page boundaries.
Reuse Semantic Models — They can run against the same shared semantic models used by interactive Power BI reports -- no separate data layer required.
For Fixed-Format Documents — Use paginated reports specifically for fixed-format, high-volume, or exportable documents, not as a general reporting default.
Different Capacity And Licensing — Paginated report capacity and licensing requirements differ from interactive reports -- confirm availability before committing a delivery plan.

modules.title: Automation, DevOps & Lifecycle Management
modules.description: Treating Power BI artifacts like source code, because eventually they have to be.
cards: PBIP and version control
Git-friendly project files that make Power BI diffable, reviewable, and mergeable.
External tools and APIs
Using the broader tooling ecosystem to script, validate, and automate what used to be manual.
CI/CD concepts for BI
Deployment pipeline thinking applied to semantic models and reports, not just application code.

topics.title: PBIP And Version Control
topics.why: A binary PBIX file is a black box to source control -- PBIP's plain-text project structure is what makes real code review and collaboration on a Power BI file possible.
bullets: Readable Folders Beat Binary — PBIP splits a report and model into readable folders and files instead of one opaque binary.
Meaningful Git Diffs — Plain-text definitions mean Git can show a meaningful diff -- what actually changed, not just 'the file changed.'
True Multi-Author Workflow — Multiple authors can work on different parts of the same solution with real merge and review capability.
Process Change, Not Just Format — Adopting PBIP is itself a process change for a team, not just a file-format setting to flip once.

topics.title: External Tools And APIs
topics.why: The Power BI ecosystem's external tools and REST APIs let teams script and validate things that used to require slow, error-prone manual clicking through the UI.
bullets: External Tool Ecosystem — External tools (Tabular Editor, DAX Studio, ALM Toolkit) extend what's possible beyond Desktop's built-in UI.
REST API For Scripting — The Power BI REST API enables scripted operations -- refresh triggers, dataset metadata, permission audits.
Safer Model Migrations — ALM Toolkit-style comparisons make model migrations and merges safer by showing exactly what will change.
Automate Repetitive Validation — Automating repetitive validation steps reduces the chance of a manual error during a release.

topics.title: CI/CD Concepts For BI
topics.why: Applying deployment-pipeline thinking to semantic models and reports catches breaking changes before they reach production, the same way it does for application code.
bullets: Automated Validation Before Deploy — A CI/CD mindset for BI means automated validation (does the model still build, do key measures still return expected results) before deployment.
Pipelines Reduce Manual Steps — Deployment pipelines or scripted release processes reduce the manual steps that introduce human error.
BI Automation Is Emerging — Automated testing for BI is less mature than for application code -- start with what can be automated today and grow from there.
Scales Module 8's Process — This module closes the loop with Module 8's repeatable release process -- automation is how that process scales past a handful of reports.

topics.title: Service Principals for Automation
topics.why: Scripted deployments and pipelines need an identity to run as -- using a personal account for that is a common shortcut that quietly becomes a security and reliability liability.
bullets: Application Identity — A service principal is an application identity, separate from any individual's account, used for automated operations.
Survives Personnel Change — Automation tied to a personal account breaks the moment that person leaves or changes roles -- a service principal doesn't have that problem.
Least Privilege — Grant a service principal only the specific permissions its automation actually needs, following least privilege.
Store Secrets In A Vault — Service principal credentials belong in a secrets manager (like Azure Key Vault), never hardcoded in a script or pipeline file.

topics.title: Fabric Workspace Git Integration
topics.why: Native Git integration connects a Fabric workspace directly to a repository -- it turns “export, commit, remember to sync” into an actual two-way, trackable connection between the Service and source control.
bullets: Auto-Sync Workspace To Branch — Workspace items sync to a connected branch automatically, keeping the repository and the live workspace aligned.
Built On PBIP Structure — This builds directly on PBIP's plain-text structure -- without it, there'd be nothing meaningful for Git to track.
Conflict Resolution Process — Conflicts between workspace changes and repository changes need a clear resolution process, the same as any team Git workflow.
Fewer Manual Export Steps — Native integration reduces manual export/import steps, which is exactly where human error tends to creep into a release process.

capstone_raw:
One dataset. One deadline.
Every skill from Modules 1-11.
Learners take a single messy source dataset from raw files to a governed, secured, production-ready Power BI solution -- end to end, without a script to follow.
Build a star schema, handle grain and role-playing dates, and validate relationships.
Write the DAX measures the business actually asked for, not the easy ones.
Design a navigable, accessible report with drillthrough and a mobile layout.
Publish, secure with RLS, and document it like it has to survive an audit.

closing.headline:
Confident modeling, defensible
numbers, and reports people trust.
closing.body:
Advanced Power BI is built for teams who are past the tutorials and need
the judgment, patterns, and habits that hold up in production.
